title: Video Streaming Platform
prompt: Design a video platform where creators upload videos and viewers anywhere can watch them smoothly on phones, laptops and TVs.

clarify.q: Is this on-demand video only, or live streaming too?
clarify.why: Live needs a sub-second ingest-to-edge path and segmenting on the fly. On-demand lets us transcode offline and pre-place files, which is a different system.

clarify.q: How long are typical uploads and how large can they get?
clarify.why: A 30-second clip can go in one request. A 2-hour 4K file (tens of GB) forces resumable chunked upload and parallel transcoding.

clarify.q: Which devices and network conditions must playback handle?
clarify.why: Phones on cellular need low rungs (240p/360p) and adaptive bitrate. Smart TVs need 1080p and above and may only support certain codecs, which sets the encoding ladder.

clarify.q: How quickly must a video be watchable after upload finishes?
clarify.why: If 'within a few minutes' is fine, we can publish the low rungs first and add high rungs later. If it must be instant, we pay for much more parallel transcoding capacity.

clarify.q: How accurate and fresh must view counts be?
clarify.why: Exact real-time counts mean a hot write path at tens of thousands per second. Counts that lag by about a minute and are deduplicated later can be aggregated in a stream cheaply.

clarify.q: Do we need DRM, private videos, or region blocking?
clarify.why: Private or paid content needs signed, expiring URLs and possibly encryption per segment, which changes how freely the CDN can cache.

clarify.q: Is recommendation and search in scope?
clarify.why: Usually not. Saying so keeps the 45 minutes on upload, transcode and delivery, where the hard parts are.

functional: A creator can upload a video up to 20 GB and resume after a dropped connection without restarting.
Uploaded videos are transcoded into several resolutions and become playable without the creator doing anything.
A viewer can start playback and the quality adapts to their bandwidth during the session.
A viewer can seek to any point and playback restarts from there within about 2 seconds.
Each video shows a view count and basic metadata (title, creator, duration, thumbnail).
nonFunctional: Playback start time under 2 s at p95 on a 5 Mbps connection.
A 10-minute upload is playable at 360p within 5 minutes of upload completing, and at all rungs within 30 minutes.
Durability of original uploads: 11 nines; never lose a creator's source file once acknowledged.
Metadata and playback APIs 99.95% available; view counts may lag by up to 1 minute.
outOfScope: Content moderation beyond a hook in the pipeline

assumptions: 200 M daily viewers, 5 views each per day = 1 B views/day
Average watch time per view: 5 minutes, delivered at an average 3 Mbps
200 k uploads/day, average length 6 minutes, source bitrate ~10 Mbps
Encoding ladder 240p/360p/480p/720p/1080p at 0.4 + 0.8 + 1.5 + 3 + 6 = 11.7 Mbps, call it 12 Mbps
Peak traffic is ~2× the daily average

steps.label: Concurrent viewers and egress
steps.math: 1 B × 300 s / 86 400 s ≈ 3.5 M concurrent; 3.5 M × 3 Mbps ≈ 10.4 Tbps
steps.result: ≈ 10 Tbps average, ~20 Tbps peak: CDN only

steps.label: Bytes delivered per day
steps.math: per view 300 s × 3 Mb = 900 Mb = 112.5 MB; × 1 B views ≈ 112 PB/day

steps.label: Raw upload ingest
steps.math: one source: 360 s × 10 Mb = 3 600 Mb = 450 MB; × 200 k = 90 TB/day; 90 TB / 86 400 s ≈ 1 GB/s

steps.label: Transcoded storage
steps.math: 360 s × 12 Mb = 4 320 Mb = 540 MB per video; × 200 k = 108 TB/day

steps.label: Transcode compute
steps.math: 200 k × 6 min = 1.2 M video-minutes/day; at ~10 core-minutes per video-minute for the full ladder = 12 M core-min / 1 440 min
steps.result: ≈ 8 300 cores busy on average, more at peak

steps.label: CDN cost at volume pricing
steps.result: ≈ $200 M/year: egress dwarfs storage and compute

estimates.takeaway: Three different scales hide in one product. Ingest is modest (~8 Gbps) and fits a regional upload tier. Transcoding is a batch compute problem of a few thousand cores that can lag a little. Delivery is ~10 Tbps and dominates cost by two orders of magnitude, so every choice about segment size, codec and cache hit ratio is really a choice about the CDN bill. Origin servers should almost never see a viewer request.

api.note: Creates an upload session. Chunk URLs are pre-signed so bytes go straight to object storage, not through our app servers.
Idempotent per index. Retrying the same chunk overwrites it, so a flaky network never corrupts the file.
The client calls this after reconnecting to learn which chunks to resend.
Assembles parts, writes the Video row, and emits VideoUploaded to start the pipeline.
Returns a CDN URL for the master playlist, signed with a short expiry for private videos.
Sent every ~30 s by the player. Feeds view counts and quality-of-experience metrics.

entities.name: Video
entities.why: Small rows, strong consistency for status changes, read by ID. 73 M rows/year is easy for Postgres.

entities.name: UploadSession
entities.why: Tracks resumable progress. A bitmap makes 'which chunks are missing' one read.

entities.name: Rendition
fields: object key of the media playlist
entities.why: One row per output. The master playlist is generated from these rows.

entities.name: ViewCount
entities.store: Counter table in Cassandra or a KV store, fed by a stream job
entities.why: Write-heavy and tolerant of lag. Kept out of the Video row so 25 k/s increments never lock metadata.

data.note: Bytes and metadata live apart. Object storage (S3-style) holds sources, segments and playlists, because they are large, immutable and served by the CDN. Postgres holds video metadata and pipeline state, because status transitions need transactions and the row count is small. The access pattern is almost always by videoId, which is the future shard key. Object keys are content-addressed per rendition, e.g. v/{videoId}/{rung}/{segment}.m4s, so they never change and can be cached forever.

hld.summary:
The upload service creates sessions and hands out pre-signed URLs, so the client sends chunks straight to object storage. On completion it writes the Video row and publishes VideoUploaded to a queue. A workflow orchestrator turns that event into a DAG of jobs: probe, split into scenes, transcode each piece per rung on a worker fleet, package into HLS/DASH segments, generate thumbnails, and finally flip the video to ready.

Viewers call the playback API once to get a manifest URL, then everything else (manifests and segments) is served from the CDN, which pulls from an origin shield in front of object storage. Player heartbeats flow into a stream processor that deduplicates sessions and updates view counters every few seconds.

diagram.title: Upload, transcode and playback paths
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  Creator[Creator app] --> UP[Upload service]
  Creator -->|chunks via signed URLs| OS[(Object storage)]
  UP --> MDB[(Video metadata DB)]
  UP --> Q[[Upload events queue]]
  Q --> ORC[Workflow orchestrator]
  ORC --> W[Transcode workers]
  W --> OS
  ORC --> MDB
  Viewer[Viewer player] --> PAPI[Playback API]
  PAPI --> MDB
  Viewer -->|manifests and segments| CDN[CDN edge]
  CDN --> SH[Origin shield]
  SH --> OS
  Viewer -->|heartbeats| SP[View count stream job]

flows.title: Uploading a 450 MB video
steps: Client calls POST /uploads; the service records a session with chunkSize 8 MB, so 57 chunks.
Client PUTs chunks directly to object storage using pre-signed URLs, 4 at a time in parallel.
Wi-Fi drops at chunk 31. On reconnect the client asks GET /uploads/{id}, sees chunks 0–30 done, and resumes at 31.
Client calls /complete. The service finalises the multipart object, writes Video(status=processing) and publishes VideoUploaded.
The creator sees 'processing'; a push notification fires when the first rung is ready.

flows.title: Watching a video
steps: Player calls GET /videos/{id}/play and receives the CDN URL of the master playlist.
Player fetches the master playlist (cached at the edge), which lists each rung with its bandwidth.
Player starts on a low rung, fetches the first 4 s segment, and starts playing as soon as it is buffered.
As measured throughput rises, the player switches to higher-rung segments at the next segment boundary.
Every 30 s it sends a heartbeat; the stream job counts the view once the session passes 30 s of watch time.

flows.title: Transcoding a new upload
steps: Orchestrator receives VideoUploaded and starts a workflow run keyed by videoId (idempotent).
Probe step reads duration, resolution and codecs, and rejects corrupt files early.
Split step cuts the source into ~30 s pieces on keyframe boundaries.
For each piece × rung, a transcode task runs on the worker fleet; 12 pieces × 5 rungs = 60 parallel tasks.
Package step stitches each rung into segments and playlists; publish step writes Rendition rows and sets status=ready.

deepDives.title: Resumable chunked upload
deepDives.problem: A 5 GB upload over a home connection at 20 Mbps takes about 33 minutes. Over that window, mobile networks change, laptops sleep and proxies time out. A single HTTP request that fails at 90% throws away 30 minutes of the creator's time. We also do not want 8 Gbps of raw video flowing through our stateless app servers.

options.name: Single PUT through our API servers
options.how: The client streams the whole file to an app server, which writes it to storage.
cons: Any failure restarts from zero
App servers proxy every byte, so we pay for bandwidth twice and must size for 8 Gbps
Long-lived requests break deploys and load balancer timeouts

options.name: Chunked upload to our own service
options.how: Client splits the file into fixed chunks, sends each with an index; our service stores chunks and tracks which arrived.
cons: Still proxies all bytes through our servers
We build and run assembly and cleanup ourselves

options.name: Pre-signed multipart upload straight to object storage
options.how: Our service opens a multipart upload, hands the client one signed URL per part, and records completed parts. On /complete it asks storage to stitch the parts.
pros: Parts retried independently and uploaded in parallel
Storage handles assembly and integrity per part
cons: Signed URLs leak if logged; keep expiry short (~1 h) and re-issue
Abandoned uploads leave orphan parts; needs a lifecycle rule to abort after 7 days

deepDives.choice: Pre-signed multipart upload with 8 MB parts. 8 MB is a balance: on a 5 Mbps mobile link a part takes ~13 s, so a retry wastes little, and a 20 GB file is ~2 560 parts, under typical multipart limits. The client hashes each part (MD5 or CRC header) so storage rejects corrupt parts, keeps a small local record of finished parts, and asks the server for the authoritative list after reconnecting. Uploads go to the nearest region and are replicated afterwards. I would switch to our own chunk service only if we needed to inspect bytes in flight, for example scanning during upload, and I would grow the part size for very large files to stay under the part-count limit.

diagram.title: Resuming after a dropped connection
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant U as Upload service
  participant S as Object storage
  C->>U: POST uploads with size 450 MB
  U->>S: start multipart upload
  U-->>C: uploadId and 57 signed part URLs
  C->>S: PUT parts 0 to 30
  Note over C,S: network drops
  C->>U: GET upload status
  U->>S: list uploaded parts
  U-->>C: parts 0 to 30 received
  C->>S: PUT parts 31 to 56
  C->>U: POST complete
  U->>S: complete multipart upload
  U-->>C: 202 videoId processing

deepDives.title: The transcoding pipeline as a DAG
deepDives.problem: Encoding a 6-minute video into five rungs serially takes about 60 core-minutes, so on one machine the creator waits a long time. A 2-hour film takes 20 times that. Steps also fail independently: a worker dies, a codec crashes on a weird frame. The pipeline must be parallel, retryable per step and idempotent, and it must let the cheap low rungs publish first.

options.name: One job per video
options.how: A worker picks VideoUploaded off the queue and runs probe, encode all rungs, package and publish in one process.
cons: Latency = full serial encode time
A crash at minute 50 redoes everything
Long videos pin one worker for hours

options.name: Queue chain with one queue per stage
options.how: Each stage consumes from its queue and publishes to the next; fan-out by emitting one message per piece × rung.
cons: Fan-in (wait for all 60 pieces) needs hand-written counters and is easy to get wrong
Hard to see where a given video is stuck

options.name: Workflow orchestrator running a DAG
options.how: A durable workflow engine (Temporal, Step Functions, or similar) runs probe → split → parallel encode per piece × rung → package per rung → publish, with retries and timeouts per task.
pros: Each task retried alone; state survives restarts
One place to see progress per video
cons: Another stateful system to run
History size per workflow grows with task count, so very long videos need child workflows

deepDives.choice: A workflow orchestrator with a DAG per video. Split the source on keyframes into ~30 s pieces, so a 6-minute video becomes 12 pieces and 60 encode tasks that finish in roughly the time of one piece. Package per rung as soon as that rung's pieces are done, and publish 240p/360p first so the video is watchable in minutes. Every task writes to a deterministic object key, which makes retries idempotent. Encode tasks run on spot or preemptible capacity because they are short and retryable, which roughly halves compute cost. If the product only had short clips under a minute, I would drop splitting and run one job per rung, because the coordination would cost more than it saves.

diagram.title: Transcode DAG for one upload
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  A[Probe and validate] --> B[Split into 30 s pieces]
  B --> E1[Encode pieces at 240p and 360p]
  B --> E2[Encode pieces at 480p and 720p]
  B --> E3[Encode pieces at 1080p]
  A --> T[Thumbnails]
  E1 --> P1[Package low rungs]
  E2 --> P2[Package mid rungs]
  E3 --> P3[Package 1080p]
  P1 --> PUB[Publish playable]
  P2 --> PUB
  P3 --> PUB
  T --> PUB

deepDives.title: Adaptive bitrate: HLS and DASH segments
deepDives.problem: Viewer bandwidth varies from 1 Mbps on a train to 100 Mbps on fibre and changes mid-session. Sending one fixed file either stalls slow viewers or wastes quality for fast ones. The player needs small, independently decodable pieces at several bitrates so it can switch without a gap. The segment length is the main knob, and it trades start time against efficiency and object count.

options.name: Short segments (2 s)
options.how: Each rung is cut into 2 s segments, each starting with a keyframe.
pros: Faster start and faster quality switches
Seek lands close to the target
cons: More keyframes cost ~5–10% bitrate at the same quality
Twice the requests and objects: 180 per rung for a 6-minute video
Per-request overhead hurts on high-latency links

options.name: Long segments (6–10 s)
options.how: Each rung is cut into 6–10 s segments.
pros: Fewer objects for the CDN to track
cons: Slower start: the first segment is bigger
Slower reaction to bandwidth drops, so more rebuffering on mobile

options.name: Medium segments in a single CMAF file per rung
options.how: 4 s fragments stored inside one fragmented MP4 file per rung, served with byte-range requests; both HLS and DASH manifests point at the same file.
pros: One encode serves both HLS (Apple) and DASH (most others)
One object per rung instead of hundreds
4 s balances start time and efficiency
cons: Byte-range caching must be supported well by the CDN
Slightly more complex packaging

deepDives.choice: 4 s CMAF fragments, one file per rung, with an HLS and a DASH manifest pointing at them. A 6-minute video becomes 90 fragments per rung. The first 240p fragment is 4 s × 0.4 Mbps = 200 KB, which downloads in about 0.3 s on a 5 Mbps link, so the 2 s start target holds. The player starts low, measures throughput per fragment, and climbs while its buffer is healthy. I would add a 2 s low-latency profile only for live or for a product where the first second matters a lot (short-form feeds). For short-form, I would also prefetch the first fragment of the next video in the feed.

deepDives.title: CDN strategy and cost
deepDives.problem: Egress is about 112 PB/day, roughly $560 k/day even at a cheap volume rate. Popularity follows a long tail: a small share of videos gets most views, while millions of videos get a few views each. Long-tail requests miss at the edge and fall through to origin, which is slow for the viewer and expensive for us.

options.name: Single commercial CDN, pull from origin
options.how: Edges cache on demand and pull misses straight from object storage.
cons: Every edge miss for a tail video hits origin; misses multiply across hundreds of edges
Highest per-GB price at our volume

options.name: Tiered caching with an origin shield
options.how: Edges pull from a few regional shield caches, which pull from origin. Popular videos are pushed to edges ahead of time.
pros: Origin sees roughly one fetch per region per object, not one per edge
Hit ratio for tail content improves a lot
cons: One more hop of latency on a miss
Shield nodes must be sized for the miss traffic

options.name: Own edge appliances inside ISPs plus commercial CDN overflow
options.how: Place cache servers inside large ISP networks, fill them overnight with predicted popular content, and use commercial CDNs for the rest.
pros: Lowest cost per GB at this scale
cons: Large up-front cost and partnerships with ISPs
Only worth it once egress is a nine-figure annual bill

deepDives.choice: Start with a commercial CDN plus an origin shield, and long cache lifetimes, since segment keys are immutable (Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable). Manifests for ready videos are also immutable. Raising the edge hit ratio from 90% to 97% cuts origin traffic by 70% (10% misses down to 3%). Use multiple CDNs with traffic steering, which helps both price negotiation and availability. Better codecs are the other big lever: AV1 or VP9 for top rungs saves roughly 30% of bytes for devices that support them, but only pays off for videos with enough views to repay the extra encode cost, so encode them only once a video crosses a view threshold. At ~$200 M/year of egress, ISP-embedded caches become worth discussing; below that I would not build them.

failures: A transcode worker dies halfway through a piece

The orchestrator times out that task and retries it on another worker. Output keys are deterministic, so a partial file is just overwritten. Alert if one video fails the same task 3 times; mark it failed and tell the creator.
A viral video sends millions of requests for the same segments at once
The CDN collapses concurrent misses into one origin fetch per edge (request coalescing), and the shield adds a second layer of collapsing. Pre-warm edges when a video trends.
One CDN provider has a regional outage
DNS or client-side steering moves traffic to the second CDN. The player retries a failed segment on an alternate host listed in the manifest.
The upload events queue backs up during a spike
Uploads still succeed because they only need storage. Processing lags; autoscale workers on queue depth and prioritise short videos and low rungs so most creators still see quick results.
A corrupt or malicious file crashes the encoder
The probe step validates container and codecs first. Encoders run sandboxed with CPU and memory limits and a hard timeout. After repeated failure, quarantine the file.
The view count stream job falls behind or restarts
Heartbeats are buffered in a durable log (Kafka-style), so the job resumes from its last offset. Counts lag but are not lost; per-session dedupe keys make replays safe.
scale: 10× views: delivery grows to ~100 Tbps. This is a CDN contract and hit-ratio problem, not an app-server one. Invest in multi-CDN steering, AV1 for popular titles, and ISP-embedded caches.
10× uploads: ~80 k cores of transcoding. Move to spot capacity with a priority queue, encode high rungs lazily for videos that get views, and consider hardware encoders for the cheap rungs.

Storage growth: ~73 PB/year now. Move sources to a cold archive tier after 30 days, and delete 1080p renditions of videos with almost no views after a year (they can be re-encoded from source on demand).
Metadata: Video rows stay small; shard Postgres by videoId once a single primary crosses a few TB, and serve video pages from a cache.

followups.q: How do you count views accurately without a hot write path?
answer: Count from player heartbeats, not from the play API, so a view means 'played at least 30 s'.
A stream job keys by sessionId to dedupe, aggregates per videoId per 10 s window, and writes one increment per video per window.
Fraud filtering (bots, replay loops) runs later in batch and can correct the count; the public number is allowed to change slightly.
Hot videos may get 10 k views/s; batching per window turns that into one write every 10 s.

followups.q: How would you support live streaming on the same system?
answer: Ingest RTMP or SRT at regional ingest servers that transcode in real time, instead of the batch DAG.
Package into 1–2 s segments and update the media playlist continuously; manifests get very short cache lifetimes.
The CDN and player stay the same, which is the main reason to standardise on HLS/DASH.

followups.q: How do you protect paid or private videos?
answer: Playback API checks access and returns a signed manifest URL that expires in minutes; edges validate the signature or a signed cookie.
For paid content, encrypt segments and hand out keys through a licence server (DRM), so a leaked URL is useless without a key.
Signed URLs reduce cache sharing only if the signature is in the cache key; strip it from the key at the edge.

followups.q: A creator replaces a video after publishing. What happens to caches?
answer: Treat it as a new version: new object keys under a new version prefix.
Update the Video row to point to the new manifest; old keys simply expire.
No purge needed, because nothing at an existing key ever changes.

followups.q: How do you pick the encoding ladder?
answer: Start with a fixed ladder for simplicity.
Then move to per-title encoding: a static lecture video looks fine at a much lower bitrate than a sports clip, so analyse complexity and choose bitrates per video.
This saves bytes on the CDN bill, which is where the money is.

mistakes: Streaming upload bytes through app servers instead of pre-signed URLs to storage.
Serving video from origin servers or treating delivery as an API scaling problem rather than a CDN problem.
Encoding one file per resolution without segmenting, so the player cannot switch quality mid-stream.
Incrementing a view count column in the metadata DB on every play.
Not estimating egress at all, and so missing that CDN cost dwarfs every other line item.

mid: Asked whether live streaming and long uploads are in scope before designing
Separated metadata (database) from video bytes (object storage)
Used a CDN for playback and explained why origin must not serve viewers
Made upload resumable with chunks and a way to ask which chunks arrived
Put transcoding behind a queue rather than in the upload request
senior: Estimated egress (~10 Tbps) and storage per day with shown arithmetic
Described the transcode DAG with split, parallel encode, fan-in and per-task retries
Explained HLS/DASH segments and adaptive bitrate, and justified a segment length with numbers
Used pre-signed multipart upload so bytes bypass app servers
Handled view counting through a stream with dedupe, not direct DB writes
Published low rungs first to meet the time-to-playable target
staff: Framed CDN cost as the dominant cost and named concrete levers: hit ratio, origin shield, multi-CDN, codec choice by popularity
Discussed long-tail versus hot content and different storage and encoding policies for each
Covered access control with signed URLs or DRM without destroying cache hit ratio
Planned the operational side: spot capacity for encodes, poison-file quarantine, pipeline observability per video
